rows.label: Conditions
rows.text: Distance is the same as displacement — Distance is the total path length (scalar, always positive). Displacement is the straight-line change in position (vector, can be zero even after traveling far). They are equal only for straight-line motion without reversal.  ·  Speed and velocity are the same — Speed is the scalar rate of distance covered ($v = d/t$). Velocity is the vector rate of displacement ($\vec{v} = \Delta\vec{r}/\Delta t$). Speed is the magnitude of velocity: $v = |\vec{v}|$.

rows.label: Limitation
rows.text: All quantities with direction are vectors — A quantity must also obey vector addition (triangle law) to be a vector. Electric current has direction but adds algebraically, so it is a scalar. Stress has direction but is a tensor, not a vector.  ·  A vector's position in space matters for equality — Two vectors are equal if they have the same magnitude and direction, regardless of where they are drawn. A free vector can be translated parallel to itself without changing its identity.

rows.label: Universal facts
rows.text: The distinction between scalars and vectors is one of the most fundamental classifications in all of physics. Every equation in mechanics, electromagnetism, and thermodynamics relies on knowing which quantities are vectors and which are scalars.  ·  Gibbs and Heaviside independently developed modern vector analysis in the 1880s, stripping it from the more cumbersome quaternion system invented by Hamilton. This made physics education dramatically more accessible.

rows.label: Study notes
rows.text: Physical quantities are classified by whether they require direction for a complete description. **Scalar quantities** have only magnitude and obey the ordinary rules of algebra (e.g., distance, speed, mass, energy). **Vector quantities** have both magnitude and direction and obey vector algebra (e.g., displacement, velocity, force, acceleration).  ·  **Scalar quantity**: a physical quantity specified completely by its magnitude alone. Examples include **mass** ($m = 5\,\text{kg}$), **temperature** ($T = 300\,\text{K}$), **speed** ($v = 60\,\text{km/h}$), and **energy** ($E = 500\,\text{J}$). Scalars add like ordinary numbers.  ·  **Vector quantity**: a physical quantity that requires both magnitude and direction for complete specification, and which obeys the triangle law of vector addition. Examples: **displacement** $\vec{s}$, **velocity** $\vec{v}$, **acceleration** $\vec{a}$, **force** $\vec{F}$. Vectors are written with an arrow, e.g. $\vec{A}$.

rows.label: More ideas
rows.text: Concept 5: Connection between Collinear and non-collinear vectors, coplanar and non-coplanar vectors and other topics  ·  Key Formula 5: Important relation in Collinear and non-collinear vectors, coplanar and non-coplanar vectors  ·  Zero magnitude means the vector has no direction at all — The zero vector $\vec{0}$ has zero magnitude but its direction is conventionally considered indeterminate. It is the additive identity: $\vec{A} + \vec{0} = \vec{A}$.

rows.label: More ideas
rows.text: Mass is a vector because it has magnitude — Mass is purely a scalar; it has magnitude but no direction. The idea of 'mass in a direction' is physically meaningless.  ·  Temperature difference is a vector because it has direction (hot to cold) — Temperature difference is a scalar. While heat flows from hot to cold, that flow direction is described by the heat flux vector, not the temperature difference itself.  ·  Any rotating quantity must be a vector — Finite rotations do not commute and therefore are not vectors. Only infinitesimal rotations obey vector addition rules. Angular velocity $\vec{\omega}$ is a vector because it represents an infinitesimal rotation rate.

rows.label: More ideas
rows.text: Electric field intensity is a scalar because it has magnitude and direction — Electric field $\vec{E}$ is a vector. Electric potential $V$ is a scalar. Don't confuse the field (vector) with the potential (scalar). The field is $\vec{E} = -\nabla V$, the gradient of the potential.  ·  Pressure exerts force in one direction only — Pressure is a scalar that acts equally in all directions. The force due to pressure on a surface element is $d\vec{F} = -p\,d\vec{A}$ where $d\vec{A}$ is the area vector perpendicular to the surface.  ·  A vector's magnitude can be negative — Magnitude is always non-negative ($|\vec{A}| \geq 0$). Negative components do not mean negative magnitude. The components $A_x, A_y, A_z$ can be negative, but $|\vec{A}| = \sqrt{A_x^2 + A_y^2 + A_z^2}$ is always positive.

rows.label: More ideas
rows.text: Scalars obey vector addition — Scalars obey ordinary algebraic addition, not vector addition. Two scalars add by simple arithmetic: $5\,\text{kg} + 3\,\text{kg} = 8\,\text{kg}$.
